questions.q: Which statement best describes supervised learning?
o: The model learns from examples that include the correct output
The model groups data without any labels
The model is programmed with explicit if–then rules
The model learns only by trial-and-error rewards
questions.ex: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples — inputs paired with the correct output.

questions.q: A bank groups customers by spending behaviour without predefined categories. This is an example of…
questions.ex: Grouping without predefined labels is clustering, an unsupervised technique.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a test set?
o: To estimate how the model performs on unseen data
questions.ex: The test set is held back so you can estimate performance on data the model has not seen.

questions.q: A model scores 99% on training data but 62% on new data. This most likely indicates…
o: Data leakage into the test set
questions.ex: A large gap between training and unseen performance is the classic sign of overfitting.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature in a model that predicts sugar-cane yield?
o: Average rainfall during the growing season
questions.ex: Features are the input variables; rainfall is an input that helps predict yield.

questions.q: Which is the best example of biased training data?
o: A face dataset drawn mostly from one age group
A dataset split 80/20 into train and test
questions.ex: Under-representing groups makes a model perform worse for them — a source of bias.

questions.q: Machine learning is best described as…
o: A separate field unrelated to AI
A subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data
Any software that uses a database
questions.ex: ML is a subset of AI focused on learning patterns from data rather than explicit rules.

o: Of all actual positives, how many did we find?
Of everything we predicted positive, how many were correct?
Predicting tomorrow's electricity demand in MW
Deciding if an email is spam

questions.q: Why should AI-generated answers in this platform show sources?
o: So learners can check them against approved course material
questions.ex: Sources let learners and lecturers verify answers against approved material.

FAQ.q: How do I reset my password?
FAQ.a: Use “Forgot password” on the sign-in page. In production this would follow the university’s identity provider (single sign-on).

FAQ.q: Can I request an extension on an assignment?
FAQ.a: Submit an academic support request with the reason and evidence. Extensions are decided by your lecturer under university regulations — the platform does not grant them automatically.

FAQ.q: Are the virtual lecturers real people?
FAQ.a: No. They are AI digital faculty. Their lessons use lecturer-approved material, and your official grades are always set by university staff.

FAQ.q: Who can see my checkpoint answers?
FAQ.a: You and the lecturers of your course. Administrators see aggregated, de-identified analytics unless they have a role-approved reason to open an individual record.

FAQ.q: What if the AI evaluation stops working during a lesson?
FAQ.a: The lesson pauses at the checkpoint, keeps your answer, and lets you retry or save and resume later. It never marks an answer correct by default.

FAQ.q: How do I turn on captions?
FAQ.a: Use the CC control in the lesson player or virtual classroom, or switch captions on by default in Profile › Accessibility.

LESSON.title: Understanding Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

segments.title: What is artificial intelligence?
speech: Artificial intelligence is the broad field of building computer systems that perform tasks we normally associate with human intelligence — understanding language, recognising images, making decisions, or planning.
Machine learning sits inside that field. Instead of a programmer writing every rule by hand, a machine learning system learns patterns from examples — from data.
And deep learning sits inside machine learning: it uses large neural networks, and it powers things like speech recognition and modern language models.
So you can picture three circles, one inside the other: AI, then machine learning, then deep learning.
simpler: Let me put it more simply. AI is the big idea: computers doing clever things that usually need a person.
Machine learning is one way of doing AI. We show the computer lots of examples, and it works out the pattern by itself.
Think of how you learnt to recognise a mango — nobody gave you a rulebook; you saw many mangoes. Machine learning works in a similar way.

checkpoint.question: Can you tell me the difference between artificial intelligence and machine learning?

concepts.label: Machine learning is a subset (part) of AI
ML learns patterns from data or examples
Without every rule being explicitly programmed
AI = systems performing tasks that need human-like intelligence

misconceptions.label: Reversed relationship — AI is not a subset of ML
They are not the same thing

hints: Here is a hint. Think about which one is the bigger idea, and which one is a particular way of achieving it.
Another clue: machine learning systems are not given every rule. Where do they get their knowledge from?
Let me be more direct. AI is the broad field. Machine learning is one part of it, where the system learns patterns from examples. Can you put that in your own words?
checkpoint.model: Artificial intelligence is the broad field of making machines perform tasks that need human-like intelligence. Machine learning is a subset of AI in which systems learn patterns from data or examples instead of following rules that were all explicitly programmed.
checkpoint.reteach: Let me explain it a different way. Imagine a university. AI is the whole university — every way of making machines act intelligently. Machine learning is one faculty inside it, the one where machines learn from examples. A chess program with hand-written rules is AI but not machine learning; a spam filter that learns from thousands of labelled emails is machine learning.

segments.title: How machine learning learns
speech: Let us look at how a machine learning system actually learns. It starts with training data — for example, thousands of emails, each already labelled spam or not spam.
The algorithm looks at the features of each example, such as words, sender and links, and adjusts a model so that its predictions match the labels as closely as possible.
This is called supervised learning, because the labels supervise the learning — they tell the model the correct answer during training.
Then we test the model on data it has never seen. If it only does well on its training data, we say it has overfitted.
simpler: Simply put: we give the computer examples with the answers attached, like a worked answer key.
It practises on those examples, checks itself against the answers, and keeps adjusting until it gets most of them right.
Then we give it new questions without the answers, to see whether it really learnt the pattern.

checkpoint.question: In supervised learning, what do the labels in the training data provide to the model?

concepts.label: The correct output / answer for each example
Used to compare predictions and correct errors during training
Pairs each input with its output so the model learns the mapping

misconceptions.label: Labels are not used in unsupervised learning; supervised learning depends on them

hints: Think of a worked answer key that a teacher gives a student. What does the key contain?
When the model makes a prediction during training, how does it know whether it was right?
Here is the core idea: each training example comes with the correct answer attached. What is the purpose of that?
checkpoint.model: The labels give the correct answer (target output) for each training example, so the model can compare its predictions with the right answers and adjust to reduce its errors.
checkpoint.reteach: Another way to see it: a label is the answer written next to each practice question. During training the model makes a guess, looks at the label, sees how wrong it was, and adjusts. Without labels it would have nothing to check itself against.

segments.title: AI in practice — and its limits
speech: Machine learning is already at work in island economies like Mauritius — forecasting electricity demand, estimating sugar-cane yields from satellite images, flagging fraudulent card transactions, and predicting tourist arrivals.
But a model is only as good as its data. If the training data under-represents some people or situations, the model can be less accurate or unfair for them. That is what we call bias.
This is why responsible AI needs human oversight, transparent sources, and testing on data that reflects everyone the system will serve.
simpler: In simple words: machine learning helps with real jobs, like predicting how much electricity people will use tomorrow.
But if we teach it with examples that leave some people out, it may make worse decisions for them.
So people must always check how these systems behave.

checkpoint.question: Optional check: give one risk of training a model on biased or unrepresentative data.

concepts.label: Unfair or less accurate results for under-represented groups

hints: Think about who might be left out of the data, and what happens when the model meets them.
checkpoint.model: The model may be less accurate or unfair for groups that were under-represented in the training data, which can lead to discriminatory decisions.
checkpoint.reteach: If a loan model only ever saw applicants from one region, it may misjudge applicants from other regions — that is the risk of biased data.

closing: Let me summarise what we covered.

Artificial intelligence is the broad field; machine learning is the part of it where systems learn patterns from data; and supervised learning uses labelled examples so the model can check itself against the correct answers.
We also saw that biased data can make models unfair, which is why human oversight matters.
For revision, I recommend the short reading on AI in everyday services, and next we will continue with supervised learning in more depth. Well done.

misconceptions.label: Treats AI and ML as the same thing
Thinks labels are the model’s predictions
Confuses bias with model error in general
